publisher: Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR)
title: USTR Takes Action in Forced Labor Section 301 Investigations
date_evidence: Press Releases - 2026 - July - USTR Takes Action in Forced Labor Section 301 Investigations ... July 23, 2026 — WASHINGTON – Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer is taking final action
key_claim: On 23 July 2026 USTR imposed final Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies for failing to impose and enforce forced-labor import prohibitions, with a 10% rate for economies that have adopted or committed to such prohibitions and 12.5% for all others, effective the day the Section 122 surcharge lapsed.
frame_summary: USTR argues that decades of moral suasion have failed to eradicate forced labor from supply chains and that conditioning tariff rates on partners adopting and enforcing US-style forced-labor import bans is both a human-rights remedy and a correction of a distortive trade practice.
verbatim_quote: Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer is taking final action, at President Trump’s direction, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 by imposing tariffs on 60 economies for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor. Today’s action comes after the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) investigations, which included two rounds of public hearings, more than 2,100 public comments, and engagement with our trading partners to remedy these longstanding concerns.
verbatim_list: 10 percent is the appropriate rate of Section 301 duties for investigated economies that (i) impose a forced labor import prohibition; (ii) have committed to impose and enforce such a prohibition through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade; or (iii) have imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods.

At the specific direction of the President, on March 12, 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative initiated 60 investigations related to the failure of various economies to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.

USTR received, reviewed, and analyzed over 1,600 written comments on the proposed responsive action. From July 7 to July 9, USTR also held public hearings regarding proposed responsive action in the investigations, at which over 100 witnesses provided testimony and responded to questions.

title: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Imposes Additional Tariffs on Canada
key_claim: On 20 July 2026 the President signed three proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 imposing additional 50% tariffs on certain Canadian goods, applying regardless of USMCA origin, exempting energy, potash and Section 232 goods, and taking effect 30 days after signing.
frame_summary: The White House frames the Section 338 action as offsetting Canadian discrimination against US cars, alcohol and dairy, presenting tariffs conditioned on partner conduct as the instrument that restores reciprocity and rewards countries that negotiate rather than retaliate.
verbatim_quote: Today, President Donald J. Trump signed three Proclamations pursuant to Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose additional 50% tariffs on certain goods of Canada in response to Canada’s discriminatory treatment of American products.
verbatim_list: These Section 338 tariffs apply to all covered goods regardless of whether a good originates under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).
These Section 338 tariffs will not apply to energy, potash, products subject to tariffs under Section 232, and certain other goods, such as fish or critical minerals.
From March 2025 through February 2026, Canadian imports of U.S. alcoholic beverages decreased by about 81%, or $582 million, compared to the same period in 2024-2025.

Over the past year and a half, only two countries have chosen to retaliate against President Trump’s tariffs rather than negotiate a deal with the United States: the People’s Republic of China and Canada.
The tariffs will take effect 30 days after signing and are designed to offset the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada’s discrimination.

title: Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs to Address Forced Labor and Excess Manufacturing Capacity (LSB11460)
date_evidence: July 21, 2026 LSB11460 — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs to Address Forced Labor and Excess Manufacturing Capacity ... Revision History Jul. 21, 2026
key_claim: CRS notes the two Section 301 investigations offer a means to reinstate tariffs on a more lasting basis than the struck-down IEEPA and expiring Section 122 measures, while flagging that challengers may invoke the major questions doctrine against tariffs covering 60 countries and that Section 301 actions terminate automatically after four years unless extended.
frame_summary: CRS frames the rebuild as legally contestable but procedurally advantaged: Section 301 explicitly authorises tariffs and survived HMTX review, yet APA review, the major questions doctrine and thin country-by-country findings give importers real litigation hooks, leaving Congress options to reassert control.
verbatim_quote: The Forced Labor Investigation and Excess Capacity Investigation potentially offer a means to reinstate tariffs on imports from multiple countries on a more lasting basis.
verbatim_list: The U.S Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February 2026, holding that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs.
Shortly after the Court’s decision, President Trump announced a global 10% tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. § 2132), which went into effect on February 24, 2026.

Tariffs and other actions taken under Section 301 terminate automatically after four years unless a petitioner or domestic industry representative requests continuation, in which case USTR may extend the action.

If Section 301 is used to impose tariffs on imports from as many as 60 countries accounting for more than 99% of U.S. imports, as proposed in the Forced Labor Investigation, challengers may argue that USTR’s action represents an “unheralded” and “transformational” use of the statute.
On June 15, 2026, the Supreme Court denied a request by the plaintiffs in HMTX Industries for certiorari (review) of the Federal Circuit’s decision.

title: Do Tariffs Ever Really Die? (The Shipment)
date_evidence: The Shipment — July 23, 2026 — Do Tariffs Ever Really Die? — Jacob Jensen
key_claim: The Section 338 tariffs on Canada target approximately $20.2 billion in imports with no USMCA exemption, Section 122's expiry ends the administration's second tariff regime after roughly $25 billion in costs, and the forced-labor Section 301 replacement would cost approximately $58.3 billion annually.
frame_summary: AAF argues the administration is building a third and perhaps final tariff regime on tested statutory authorities, quantifies the cost of each instrument, and expects the untested Section 338 to face the same court challenges that ended IEEPA.
verbatim_quote: The tariff authority the administration is using is found in Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent or to fully block trade if a country discriminates against U.S. goods.
verbatim_list: First, the Section 338 tariffs target approximately $20.2 billion in U.S. imports, or about 5 percent of all imports from Canada.
At midnight, the 10-percent Section 122 tariffs currently in place on a wide variety of imports will expire, marking the end of the Trump Administration’s second tariff regime.
The Shipment estimates that the 10-percent Section 122 tariffs will have raised costs for U.S. businesses and consumers by $25 billion over the 150 days it was in effect.
Previous AAF research estimates that these tariffs alone would cost U.S. consumers and businesses approximately $58.3 billion annually given 2025 import data.
The Section 338 tariffs are scheduled to go into effect 30 days after President Trump’s proclamation, meaning August 19 is the deadline for U.S.-Canada negotiations to prevail.

The fact Section 338 has not been utilized by any president in the past combined with the argument that more recent Section 301 tariff authorities supersede 338 indicates it may be a hard-fought legal battle for the Trump Administration once again.

title: Replacing IEEPA Tariffs (The Shipment)
date_evidence: The Shipment — March 19, 2026 — Replacing IEEPA Tariffs — Jacob Jensen
key_claim: The March 2026 Section 301 investigations covered 86 separate countries representing just over 99 percent of 2025 US import value, an unprecedented simultaneous use of the statute, and together with eight ongoing Section 232 investigations they will create a patchwork of tariffs that somewhat replaces the IEEPA regime.
frame_summary: AAF argues the trade team is deliberately rebuilding the struck-down IEEPA regime brick by brick on legally tested authorities, in part to restore leverage over partners whose deals were negotiated under the old tariffs and have no legislative ratification.
verbatim_quote: The new Section 301 investigations cover 86 separate countries – of which 16 are double targeted – representing just over 99 percent of the total U.S. import value in 2025. This marks an unprecedented use of Section 301 as there have never been this many simultaneous investigations on this many countries.
verbatim_list: The combination of Section 232 and Section 301 activity will slowly create a patchwork of tariffs that somewhat replace the IEEPA regime.
By contrast, Sections 232 and 301 are far more reliable and are unlikely to be struck down by U.S. courts unless the administration fails to follow the formal investigation processes.
In addition to current and future Section 301 investigations, there are also eight ongoing Section 232 investigations that will cover a wide swath of U.S. imports in the name of national security.

title: New Tariff Relief Path for Pharmaceutical Companies That Negotiate Onshoring Agreements
date_evidence: May 19, 2026 — New Tariff Relief Path for Pharmaceutical Companies That Negotiate Onshoring Agreements — Holland & Knight Alert
key_claim: Under Proclamation 11020 the default Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff is 100 percent from 31 July 2026 for large companies, but Commerce-approved onshoring agreements cut the rate to 20 percent and pairing them with HHS most-favored-nation pricing agreements takes it to zero through 20 January 2029.
frame_summary: The law firm frames the pharma tariff as a relief-for-commitments bargain: the punitive headline rate exists so that companies buy it down with audited onshoring investment plans and government pricing agreements, with Commerce monitoring compliance and able to reimpose tariffs retroactively.
verbatim_quote: The standard Section 232 tariff rate for pharmaceuticals is 100 percent, but companies with approved onshoring plans qualify for a 20 percent rate and, if they also enter into most favored nation (MFN) pricing agreements with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), won't pay a Section 232 tariff at all.
verbatim_list: In Proclamation 11020, issued on April 2, 2026, President Donald Trump determined that imports of certain pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients threaten to impair U.S. national security and imposed tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

The Proclamation sets a default 100 percent tariff rate for covered patented products and associated ingredients, effective July 31, 2026, for certain large companies and September 29, 2026, for small companies, while excluding generic pharmaceuticals and their associated ingredients.

It also delegates authority to the Secretary of Commerce to enter into company-specific onshoring agreements that qualify approved companies for a 20 percent tariff rate, with a zero percent rate through January 20, 2029, for companies that also execute MFN pricing agreements with HHS.

title: 60 economies, two tariff tiers, and one deadline that's already passed: Is your trade team ready for the next wave?
key_claim: The Section 301 forced-labor action covers 60 economies accounting for 99.4% of US imports, took effect at 12:01 a.m. on 24 July 2026 with an in-transit exception closing 28 July, applies an MFN-rate cap rather than a flat add-on for five economies, and does not stack with Section 232 duties.
frame_summary: The vendor frames the action as an operational compliance shock: near-total country coverage with product-level, entry-level rate complexity that makes manual tracking unworkable, used to argue for its trade-content software.
verbatim_quote: the Section 301 tariff action covers 60 economies that, together, account for 99.4% of all U.S. imports
verbatim_list: The tariffs took effect July 24, 2026, at 12:01 a.m. Eastern, with a narrow in-transit exception that closed July 28.

Economies with a full or partial forced-labor import ban, or a reciprocal-trade commitment, face a 10% additional duty. That group includes India, the UK, and Mexico, among others. Everyone else faces 12.5%, including China, Brazil, and the EU.
USTR has indicated it won’t be feasible until around September 1, 2026, so the 10% duty applies until then.
